result.question:
I have a feeling we keep fixing the same fault on Transformer 1 at site MAIN without ever getting to the root cause. Check that for me.

Pull all closed work orders on Transformer 1 with their number, description, completion date and failure code. Use our failure code catalog to map each one to a transformer fault type: partial discharge, low-energy arcing, high-energy arcing, oil overheating, core or winding thermal fault, tap changer wear, moisture ingress, cellulose ageing or oil dielectric degradation.

Then work out what the transformer is doing now. Run a dissolved gas fault classification on the latest complete sample between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 using hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene, and use co from the same sample to check whether the paper is involved. Map that result to the same list of fault types.

Call it a recurring fault only if at least two closed work orders map to the same fault type the gases show today.

If it's recurring:
- Check open work orders on Transformer 1 for an existing root cause investigation or manufacturer referral. If there is one, give me its number and don't duplicate it.
- Otherwise, create a priority 2 root cause investigation work order. List the earlier work order numbers in the notes, add a note to notify the manufacturer, and code it with the matching failure code.

If only one earlier job matches, don't create anything. Recommend a confirmatory oil resample and say that one repeat isn't enough to call a pattern. If none match, say today's fault looks new.

If a closed work order has no failure code, map it from its description and mark it as inferred. Inferred matches can support a recurrence but can't be the only basis for one. If the latest sample is missing any of the five gases, use the most recent complete sample and give its timestamp.
result.answer:
**Verdict: Not a recurring fault — there is no closed work-order history on Transformer 1 to recur against. Today's fault looks new.**

## 1. Closed work orders on Transformer 1 (site MAIN)

None. I queried all statuses, then `COMP` and `CLOSE` explicitly — all returned zero closed work orders. The only work order on the asset is:

| WO | Description | Status | Completion date | Failure code | Mapped fault type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1000051 | OLTC inspection – on-load tap changer (suspected contact wear/coking) | APPR (open, PdM, priority 1) | — (not completed) | none | tap changer wear *(inferred from description)* |

Because it is open, it cannot count toward a recurrence. Note also that the catalog (FC001–FC010) is generic — the closest transformer-relevant code is FC006 "overheating or high temperature reading"; none map cleanly to discharge, moisture, or ageing faults.

## 2. What the transformer is doing now

Latest complete sample: **2024-01-18T00:00:00** (all five gases + CO present; every sample in the window was complete).
H2 2900 · CH4 7350 · C2H6 5450 · C2H4 16600 · C2H2 7 · CO 33 ppm

The `interpret_dga` tool returned "LLM unavailable" on two attempts, so I computed the IEC 60599 Rogers Ratios directly:

| Ratio | Value | IEC code |
|---|---|---|
| C2H2 / C2H4 | 7 / 16600 = 0.0004 | 0 |
| CH4 / H2 | 7350 / 2900 = 2.53 | 2 |
| C2H4 / C2H6 | 16600 / 5450 = 3.05 | 2 |

Code **0-2-2 → T3, thermal fault > 700 °C** (high confidence: ethylene-dominant, negligible acetylene rules out arcing; CH4/H2 > 1 rules out partial discharge). TDCG ≈ 32,340 ppm — IEEE C57.104 Condition 4, severe.

**Paper involvement:** CO is only 33 ppm against ~32,000 ppm of hydrocarbons. CO that low means cellulose is essentially not participating — this is a bare-metal / oil hot spot, not insulation degradation.

**Mapped fault type: core or winding thermal fault** (T3, metal overheating — e.g. circulating currents, bad core-ground or lead connection, or a hot OLTC contact in the main tank).

## 3. Recurrence test

Closed work orders mapping to "core or winding thermal fault": **0** (there are no closed work orders at all). Threshold is ≥ 2, so this is **not recurring**, and I have **not created any work order**.

## Recommendations

- **Today's fault looks new** from a records standpoint — but the gas levels are severe, not a wait-and-see condition. The existing open **WO 1000051** (OLTC inspection, priority 1, approved) is already on the asset and already carries a note to take a confirmatory DGA sample. That is the right vehicle; I'd suggest widening its scope to include core-ground and bushing/lead connection checks, since CO says the paper is clean and the T3 signature could be main-tank metal rather than the OLTC.
- Your "fixing the same fault" feeling may be right, but the evidence isn't in this system — prior repairs may have been recorded under a different asset number, site, or before the current database. If you can point me to where older records live, I'll re-run the recurrence check against them.
